The same is true with patience and perfection.
Choose to be patience as you wait for your people to get on board with something.
Stick to the facts as you remind them of what matters, and do it patiently.
Learning new things and applying them is no joke.
Which is why it’s important to remember that you don’t hold all the solutions.
You are not the smartest person in the room all the time.
Be humble and collaborative when something isn’t working.
Bring your people into it rather than creating different boundaries and rules and incentives to use your system.
And if something matters that much to you, just do it yourself.
If you can’t lower your expectations or you struggle to be patience as things stay inconsistent, be prepared to do it yourself, kindly and warmly because no one needs a passive aggressive bedfellow.
And finally let all of this teach you to be content.
Let it remind you that not everything has to be optimized and awesome.
Some things in your house will stumble along.
Some systems will take years to find their way.
I’ve had to learn to be content with a giant green mower battery sometimes being on my pretty vintage mail table because Kaz needs to charge it and won’t remember if it’s not out.
That big ol’ green battery has practically been a spiritual teacher for me.
Because guess what?
It doesn’t matter.
I can be content that Kaz needs the visual reminder of the battery by the door.
I can relax around how extremely large this battery is.
I can stop trying to change how his brain works and just be content.
I can also notice that the battery has been there four days and feel myself going a little crazy by it and then stick to the facts and talk to Kaz.
“Hey, babe.
What’s your plan for the battery?

Because your girl is starting to see it in her sleep. ” And he laughs because he knows that the green battery irritates me but also does what he can to remove it from the pretty table as soon as possible.
It’s far too easy to carry resentment when your people don’t follow your plan.
It’s far too easy to assume the solution is to get them on board.
It’s not.
The solution is from within you.
Assume the best, stick to the facts, don’t keep score, choose people over productivity, patience over perfection, collaborate or just do it yourself, and be content.
And that’s what to do when your people don’t follow the plan.

After the break, we’ll have an Office Hours about corralling all the library books, and we’ll celebrate the Lazy Genius of the Week with a great idea on sharing the mental load of shopping with your partner.
We’ll be right back! *** AD BREAK *** Our Office Hours question this week comes from Michelle from Toronto, Canada.
Michelle asks: "I need some help to Lazy Genius my kids books, but especially their library books.

My kids (ages 10 and 4) love to read and visit the library, but their books end up *everywhere* and it makes library book return day SO stressful, especially since we don't just take out a few books - we max out the cards (that's 50 books.
And shockingly we do get through them all before return day!).

The library books are mostly contained to the living room, which is where they do the most reading, and I take a picture of the spines of the library book before we bring them home so I have a reference to look at when they inevitably scatter or end up under furniture.
I've tried having a basket for the books to live in but it never lasts long.
They unfortunately end up piled all over the couch and coffee table, making it hard to use the living room for anything other than book storage.

While I recognize that having avid readers who read too much is a good problem to have, what matters most to me is having a comfortable space to read together, and being able to return books on time, because library day shouldn't be so stressful!
Please help!" Okay, I love a problem of too many books.

My first instinct is to use a combination of two Lazy Genius principles - The Magic Question, i.e. what I can do to make this easier later and Build the Right Routines where you’re not worried so much about a specific order of tasks but with where you’re trying to go.
Michelle, you said library day twice.
That makes me think you have a set day you go to the library with your kids, whether that’s the actual book return day or a specific day of the week.
You already do such a thorough job of keeping up with what you checked out and what day it all goes back, so I’m wondering if you shift when you gather books from library day to a different day.
If you know when library day is, magic question gathering the books and build a routine the day before library day where you’re not in a rush, you’re trying to get back home before lunch or whatever.
It’s just a task the day or two before where everyone starts gathering library books into the basket you’ve already tried.
You said the basket doesn’t last long.
Totally great.
What if its job was not to hold the books the entire couple of weeks but just the day or two before library day?
That’s its job.
That’s the place for all the books leading up to library day.

So if you know you’re going to the library this Wednesday because it’s when the books are due, on Tuesday you say to your kids, “tomorrow is library day, so let’s take five minutes now to find as many library books as we can and put them in the basket in the living room. ” And then the bulk of the work is done.
You have time to reference the photo you took if you’re missing a few from the count, and you’re not in a rush to get out the door to go to the actual library.
I think that could potentially solve the library day gathering problem.
The books around the living room problem is different.
And my thought there is to make stacks your friend.
When books are everywhere and there are either too many to live in a basket or used so often that they don’t consistently make it to the basket, stacks are your friend.
Maybe once or twice a day, you and the kids do a quick stack time.
“Hey, crew, if you see books around that aren’t in a basket, make a stack please!” Just get used to stacking the books.
Stacks look tidier than anything spread out, so if you’re hoping for a bit less visual chaos in your living room but you still want the books there, make stacks.
Use the basket whenever it works, but ultimately use stacks.
And to the point of the basket, you said “I’ve tried having a basket for books to live in, but it never lasts long. ” Maybe view the basket less as a constant home and more of a periodic one.
The books are out.
They’re being used.
They’re doing what they’re supposed to which you seem mostly at peace with.
But I think that sometimes we expect a storage solution to work all the time or if it’s not working all the time, then it’s not working.
And that’s just not true.
Even if the basket holds fifty percent of the books fifty percent of the time, it’s still a helpful place to put books.
So maybe lower your expectations on the consistency of the basket and use it whenever it helps.
If that’s not always, that’s fine.
Thanks for your question, Michelle, and I hope this helps!
And now for Lazy Genius of the week!
This week we have Cindy from Lexington.
Cindy writes: "Years ago my partner and I would text each other before stopping at the grocery to ask if there were any requests or needed items.
It was not a great system and the timing often didn't work to respond on time.
Thus, there would often be frustrations with items not getting purchased or one person feeling like it was their responsibility to take stock of what was needed.
I discovered a basic shared "our groceries" list app that has been a game changer to share the mental load and work ever since.
If an item is getting low then it's the person's responsibility to add it to the shared grocery list.
If one of us does a grocery run, you can click on the item as it's added to the shopping cart so we know it has been purchased.
In addition to Kroger, we have Costco, Trader Joe's and Lowe's lists.
We also have a few lists that we don't use as often but come in handy to remember and add to as needed.
For example, we have a "fix it" list for our handy person since we only contact him when there are enough items worth having him come fix around the house.
We also have a doctor's list where we add notes to discuss with our own doctors or with a kid's pediatrician as an annual visit approaches.
Again, you can customize it for your personal, couple, and family needs.
Now I cannot imagine living without this tool.
Hope this can help someone share and distribute the shopping and household work load. " Well, this is great.
I love how this grew from groceries to other things as well, to doctors and handyman lists.
I imagine too that this would be helpful in a home with teenagers who can drive and also have access to phones when they might go to the store for something, too.
I’m not sure what this specific app is that Cindy uses, but you can totally use your Notes app on iphones.
Not sure what an Android equivalent would be, but for both you could use Google docs or anything shared.
So many native apps have sharing options where everybody can update and see the same list.
Goodness knows I have been in that texting neverland where you’re asking if somebody needs something and no one texts back in time, so this is a great option.
If you think this would help you, I encourage you to start small.
Start with one type of list, not all the ones that Cindy uses.
My guess is that Cindy and her husband did not create all of these lists at once.
The grocery one probably worked well over a period of time to the point where they saw the benefit of adding another kind of list.
So start small if this sounds like an idea you can get behind, and thanks for sharing, Cindy, and being our Lazy Genius of the Week!
In the next podcast recap email, I’m going to share the three rules from Jackie’s book So I Married a Human that Kaz and I are excited to use in our own marriage.
If you’d like to get that email, you can sign up at thelazygeniuscollective.com/recap.
It goes out every other Thursday.
And in the next monthly newsletter which goes out this Wednesday, I’ll answer a question somebody sent in about how to enter a new season of having a baby.
I haven’t talked about that specifically in a long time and definitely not here on the podcast.
I do have a podcast episode called The Lazy Genius Raises a New Baby, and it was - wait for it - the 18th episode I ever did.
So we have gone 470 podcast episodes without talking about babies.

Which makes sense because it’s a specific season that’s short lived and not happening to everyone, but in case you are someone who is in that season or about to be, you might want some updated words about new baby times.
If that’s the case and you’re not already subscribed to our monthly newsletter list, now would be a great time. thelazygeniuscollective.com/join.
If this episode was helpful to you, share it with someone you know or leave a review on Apple Podcasts.
Both are small ways to support the show but hugely helpful to us, so thank you for your support.
This podcast is part of the Audacy family and the Office Ladies Network.
This episode is hosted by me, Kendra Adachi, produced by Leah Jarvis, and executive produced by Kendra Adachi, Jenna Fischer, and Angela Kinsey.
Thanks, y’all, for listening, and until next time, be a genius about the things that matter and lazy about the things that don’t.
I’m Kendra, and I’ll see you next week.

episodes.title: A Fall Bucket List (But Better)

cues.text: #488 - A Fall Bucket List (But Better) Welcome to The Lazy Genius Podcast where we all get to be a genius about the things that matter and lazy about the things that don’t.
Every Monday, you’ll learn to compassionately manage your time, wisely solve problems, and kindly live in your season.
I’m your host, Kendra Adachi, and I’m so glad you’re here.
Today is Episode 488: A Fall Bucket List (But Better).
Why better?
Well, bucket lists, while wonderful, also carry a lot of pressure and frankly morbidity to them.
I mean, the origin is from the phrase “kick the bucket” which means to die.
And while I think it’s great to have a list of things you’d love to do before you die, that’s a less appropriate list when you just want to enjoy October.

Also since one of the 13 Lazy Genius principles is to live in your season and many of us are living in fall or about to once the temperature goes down, let’s take a little time to make sure we’re enjoying the parts of this season that we love, that make us feel happy and alive, and that usually are limited to only fall.
I want the things you love about this season to actually make it onto your calendar and into your life.
When that happens, the stuff you have to do feels lighter and better, and you have more emotional capacity to be present and enjoy where you are.
So today we are going to create a better list for fall – your fall favorites.
Let’s make a list of favorite things you love about fall – things you want to eat, drink, cook, see, smell, watch, listen to, and do before we hit Thanksgiving.
And then the important thing is making sure they happen.
Making the list probably isn’t going to be that hard.
In fact, that’s the fun part.
But how can we ensure your fall favorites actually happen?
I’ve got some ideas to incorporate your fall favorites into your life.
In some ways, this episode is like What’s Saving My Life in reverse.
We’re preemptively putting things into our fall lives that make life feel really good.
I’m excited.
So let’s set the stage just a little bit for this season.
The wide expanse of time between summer and the winter holidays is stereotypically a favorite time of year.
September but especially October and the beginning of November.
People love fall.
You’re in a routine, but you’re not overwhelmed by Thanksgiving and Christmas yet.
Maybe the weather is cooling down but not freezing, and it’s just a good time.
There are so many things that feel like they belong in October and nowhere else.
And also the fall season can feel so busy.
Kids’ sports and school activities.
Some workplaces start to get a little crazy at the start of Q4 to hit the annual goals that still have a ways to go.
And October often flies by.
It holds so much fun and coziness and magic, but it can also be gone in a blink because there aren’t big holiday anchors, and suddenly we realize we didn’t enjoy the season the way we hoped to.
This quote from J.R.R.
Tolkien is our guide today: “Do not spoil the wonder with haste!” Legolas says this to Gimli in The Return of the King, and I’m saying it to you now.
Do not spoil the wonder with haste!
Let’s take our time this fall season enjoying what we love about it, what the season offers, and how we can experience it in a way that matters.
So let’s make our fall favorites list!
Obviously yours will be different from mine and everyone else listening, but I do want to give you some ideas and categories to think about.
What I’d love is for you to take a little bit of time over the next couple of days and keep a list of what your fall favorites are.
As things come to mind or as you do a little research on what movies you want to watch or whatever, put them on your list.
You won’t leave this episode with a list per se, but you will leave with tools to make one and get it done.
Now before we get into making your list, I want to lay down a few ground rules.
You need to keep these things in mind so that you don’t turn into a fall memory robot, okay?
One, say yes to what matters first.
That’s the point of today’s episode, to name what your favorites are so you can actually say yes to them.
It doesn’t mean the other things won’t happen, but it’s so important that you say yes to what matters first so they definitely will.
Two, a no right now isn’t a no forever.
There may be things that you love about fall that can’t happen this year for some reason outside of your control.
Just because you have to let something go this year doesn’t mean you’re letting it go forever.
Now isn’t forever.
Three, be careful about manufacturing memories.
We’re creating space for enjoyable fall things to happen, but hold a loose grip on how things go or how your people react to them.
You can’t manufacture memories, so take a breath and relax.
You’ll have more fun that way anyway.
Four, combine senses.

When you link sensory experiences, like listening to fallish music while also lighting a candle or having a mug of something spicy and warm next to you, even if you’re doing work or chores, it enhances everything.
You’re injecting fall into your season in a tangible, tactile way, and it’s pretty great.
Almost immersive.
And five which is basically a repeat of one, please oh please choose the most important thing from each category, not everything.
It’s fine to make a long list of recipes you want to make.
Of course.
But as you make your list, make sure you’re starring or prioritizing one thing in each category.
It’s a gift you’re giving yourself, because if you do just that one thing and nothing else on your list, it’ll still feel like fall.
You’ll still have done your favorite thing and loved it.
So even though making this entire favorites list is fun and I hope you get to enjoy everything, be aware of starting small.
Start with one thing that’s the most important thing so you’re more likely to actually do it.
Okay, let’s jump in.
I’ll share some typical categories and my favorite thing from within them as you think about yours.
Let’s start with fall beverages.
There are so many to choose from – the PSL, certain kinds of beer, apple cider, hot chocolate.
The thing that I love to drink in the fall the most is golden milk.
Or my own version of it.
There’s an old post on my Instagram page that shares how I make it, but it’s basically brewed spiced tea with turmeric, any extra spices I want, and a generous pour of creamy milk.
I love both oat milk and heavy cream.
It makes this absolutely luscious golden drink that’s warm and spicy and creamy and super delicious.
And something I only want to drink in October and November.
I don’t care that much about drinking special fall lattes or making homemade cider.
I mean, if they’re there, I’ll enjoy them, but my fall favorite is golden milk.
So that’s the only beverage going on my list because it’s my favorite and I want to make sure I enjoy it.
What about foods?
Your fall favorite food might be soup or some other comfort food like chicken pot pie.
Or maybe it’s an ingredient, like apple anything or pumpkin anything.
Maybe your fall favorite food is tied to an experience, like baking pie or roasting marshmallows or having a huge pancake dinner with maple syrup.
Mine is chili and homemade cornbread.
I usually make it about three times throughout October and November, and it makes me so happy.
I’ll be sure to include the recipe in the next newsletter, too.

I think I have before like a year or two ago, but if you want my cornbread that’s a little sweet which is how I like it, sign up for the newsletter at thelazygeniuscollective.com/join or just find your own favorite cornbread recipe and make it.
But that’s the fall food I’m prioritizing.
The other stuff is fine if and when it happens, but I am most definitely prioritizing chili and homemade cornbread in my cast iron skillet because it is without question my fall favorite.
Again, I highly encourage you take the same approach.
What’s your absolute favorite or small set of favorites that have to happen?
Prioritize those, and you’ll feel like fall is most definitely fall.
So that’s food and drink.
What about sensory vibey things?
What’s your favorite fall aesthetic?
Is it lit candles that smell of things like pine and sandalwood?
Is it wearing cozy socks around the house?
Lots of blankets?
Flannel?
Sweatshirts?
Bonfires in the front yard?
Name your favorite thing so you can be sure to do it.
Mine is the homesick North Carolina candle.
The company homesick does all kinds of scents tied to places and vibes.
I’ve never smelled one I didn’t love, and their fall scents are so great.
But my absolute favorite will forever be the North Carolina candle.
The state candles are so great, but they nailed the North Carolina candle so well.
Homesick shares the notes of all their candles, and this one has top notes of blackberry, peach, and tobacco.
You can really smell the tobacco, and coming from a state and a family that farmed tobacco for generations, it smells like home.
Mid notes of cinnamon, sugar, and clove, and base notes of vanilla, amber, and tonka bean.
I think the tobacco and tonka bean ground what could be a spicy candle, but the combination is just the most perfect fall smell on the planet.
It is without question my favorite fall aesthetic, and I don’t really burn it until October.
It doesn’t fit in July.
It belongs in October.
I lit it for the first time about two weeks ago even though it was 95 degrees outside because I just couldn’t wait any longer.
Once we drop below 75, that thing is going to be burning constantly.
I also have to mention sweatshirts in here.
Such a slow pitch and not hard to incorporate into life at all, but I am such a fan of crewneck sweatshirts.
I have too many and also I need more.
I just love them and wear them almost every day once it gets cool enough to.
It’s not a fall favorites list for me without mentioning sweatshirts.
So what’s your fall favorite aesthetic?
What’s the sensory aesthetic you really love and don’t want to do without?
Prioritize the favorite so it really happens.
One fall aesthetic that’s easy to add that deserves its own categorical mention is music.
Music requires very little effort and just plays in the background, enhancing whatever you’re doing with great fall vibes.
So pay attention to music in your life when you can, or name if there are albums you love to listen to in the fall.
One of mine is Pink Moon by Nick Drake.
A classic and belongs in the fall.
I love listening to it only a couple of months a year because it transports me so much.
I save it on purpose and love that I do.
Some other ideas: Nat King Cole for Fall: Autumn Leaves.
It’s some remastered songs that super duper feel like fall, as does his voice.
I love Nat King Cole.
Shore by Fleet Foxes is so fall I can hardly stand it.
A winner in every way.
Ella Fitzgerald is a great fall artist.
I like to double up with Ella and Louis, the album with her and Louis Armstrong.
Vibes for days.
Lowland Hum is another band that has great fall vibes no matter the album.
I love all their stuff, but Thin is probably my favorite album and super fallish.
Pumpkin by Georgia Parker.
For Mary by Olive Jones.
Iron and Wine.
Sufjan Stevens.
Nina Simone.
Music is just the best way to add a fall aesthetic.
And of course Breezy Instrumental, my most popular playlist forever, will be a lovely fall companion to your ears. [ad break] Now let’s think about activities.
What are your fall favorite activities that you try to do every year that are your favorite thing about the season?
Getting a beer at a local brewery and being outside in a sweater.
Walking in the woods as the leaves change.
Going to a pumpkin patch or carving pumpkins.
Buying mums from the farmers market.
Apple picking.
Jumping in a pile of leaves.
Camping.
S’mores.
High school football.
The state fair.
A corn maze.
So many of these things only happen in October and November, so it’s a blast to name the thing you love the most so you can make sure it happens.
I’ve mentioned this a million times, but our fall opening ceremony has been the same for like fifteen years.
It doesn’t really and truly feel like fall until we do this.
We go to a local farm and do their corn maze and hay ride and then buy pumpkins from them.
Then we get Culvers custard on the way home since we only have one Culvers close by and it’s that one but still pretty far from where we live.
We’ve gone since Sam was little, kept adding our own kids, and in the last few years, other people’s kids so our kids have friends.
Just the other day, Sam my oldest who’s a junior in high school was like “Hey, when are we going to the corn maze this year?
I’m trying to think about who I want to invite. ” It’s just what we do, and it’s such a good time.
We have a million pictures of our family at the start of the corn maze, and it’s like a little walk down memory lane.
I love the other fall experiences I listed, especially high school football.
Man do I love high school football.
But that is built into our lives already because my boys are in the marching band and we go to the games anyway.
The corn maze is different.
We’ve got to carve out time to do that over a weekend, and without it, fall just isn’t real.
The other stuff I listed is a fun bonus if it happens, but it doesn’t have to happen.
I’m going to spend my planning energy making sure our favorite thing happens.
So what’s your fall favorite activity that you want to make sure you plan?
Prioritize the one thing so you can make sure it happens.
Let’s talk about one more category: shows, movies, and books.
Some people love to reread or rewatch certain things in the fall, and other people have things they’re looking forward to enjoying for the first time this fall.
You might always watch It’s the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown or the first season of Gilmore Girls.
Practical Magic, When Harry Met Sally, Little Women, Harry Potter, You’ve Got Mail.
All of these and a million more feel like they belong in the fall.
So maybe choose if there’s a show, movie, or book that is your fall favorite and you want to make sure you watch or read it this month.

It’s probably way better to choose just one from each category if you’re already tight on time so you can make sure it happens, but you also might be a person who has a whole list of things you’re going to binge and will absolutely get them done.
I love that for you.
I will almost certainly reread The Ocean at the End of the Lane this October.
It’s by Neil Gaiman and one of my favorite books of all time.
It’s short, weird, and atmospheric, about a boy who thinks his dad’s new wife is an evil creature from another dimension and sets out to destroy her with the help of some magical friends.
It’s so good.
I love it with my whole heart.
But do you know what else I love that I haven’t read in forever?
A couple of books actually.
The Night Circus by Erin Morgenstern is such a fall book and one of my favorites ever.
I haven’t reread it in years and might this year.
We’ll see.
Same goes for Till We Have Faces by C.S.
Which reminds me, I have reread The Chronicles of Narnia in the fall before.

There are so many great books that feel like they deserve to be read in the fall, so if you have a book you love that fits that category, see if that’s something you might want to add to your fall favorites.
What about shows and movies that are coming out soon?
That’s a fun list to make, too.
I don’t know about you, but I let new shows and movies that I’m looking forward to just slide on by.
They are the hardest to incorporate into life for various reasons, and it always makes me sad.
Like, y’all, I still haven’t seen Project Hail Mary.
Mostly because Ben wants to see it too as does Kaz, but it’s hard to find something that the three of us can do that Sam and Annie aren’t around for.
But that is something I really want to do this fall!
Watch Project Hail Mary!
I also want to see the new Sense and Sensibility with Daisy Edgar Jones.
The one with Emma Thompson remains my favorite movie of all actual time, but I am still excited about this version.
Hoping to make it to the actual theater for this one.
I’m pumped about the show Below that’s coming out on Netflix in a couple of weeks.
It’s Josh Hartnett, Mackenzie Davis, and Charlie Heaton in what feels like a mix between Stranger Things and Midnight Mass.
I typically avoid stories with boats and oceans, but this one has me super pumped.
Season four of The Diplomat comes out in the middle of October, and I will be locked in on that one.
And of course the new season of Bakeoff.
Annie and I have had that on the calendar for awhile.
But here’s the thing about books, shows, and movies.
Make your list of things that are fun to rewatch or reread or experience for the first time, but pair those experiences with other fall things.
Make hot toddies.
Bake a pie.
Eat chicken soup.
Sit under blankets.
Light candles.
Eat caramel popcorn.
Do things that enhance the experience of the watching or reading, and it will be so very fallish it’ll make you so stinkin happy.

Okay, to recap, here’s my list of fall favorites that I want to make sure happen: golden milk, chili and cornbread, the North Carolina candle, sweatshirts, Pink Moon and honestly a ton of other fall music, corn maze day, high school football, rereading The Ocean at the End of the Lane, going to see Sense and Sensibility, and watching Project Hail Mary and Below at home.
Below feels like fall whereas The Diplomat just happens to be coming out in the fall.
I could watch that any time even though I will most certainly watch it in October when it comes out.
But that’s my list.
Okay, now let’s talk about making these things happen practically.
Once you have your list, I hope it’s not super long so that you can actually do it.
Keep it to your favorites if you can.
Or just star the ones that matter the most so you don’t have a list of 25 unprioritized things you’re trying to do.
Keep it small and doable so that the enjoyment actually happens.
Now when you have your list, you’ll have things that will naturally happen, like me and high school football, and others that need planning or might else they might not happen.
Start with those things.
Start with the things that need a little bit of troubleshooting.
What might keep you from doing that thing?
When you name the obstacle, it’s easier to work around it.
Our corn maze is the biggest thing that’s likely to not happen, just because of how quickly weekends fill up.
So I already put a placeholder event on the calendar so the day doesn’t fill up.
It’s not locked in yet, but it’s got a place to start from.

Your obstacle might not be logistics like mine is, but when you name the thing that’s most likely to keep you from doing your favorite thing, you’re more likely to find a solution before it’s too late.
So look at your list, notice the things that are less likely to happen without a little help, name what could keep it from happening, and put something in place to prevent that.
Next, schedule what can be scheduled.
Put stuff on the calendar.
For me, I’m going to put chili and cornbread on the meal calendar later in October once it’s hopefully colder outside.
The corn maze day is currently on the calendar and might not have to move.
We’ve got a night coming up soon where Sam is gone for a school thing, so I’m going to put Project Hail Mary movie night on the calendar that night.
Hopefully it’ll happen, but it won’t unless I schedule it.
Same for Below.
It comes out the first week of October, but we’ve got a lot of stuff going on that week.
The week after though, I have it on my calendar with a question mark on my day off.
I might just do a binge watch and eat soup and drink golden milk under a blanket and have the best time.
The point is it’s scheduled.
So do that with your list.
Schedule what can be scheduled.
Some things don’t need that, but schedule what does.
If you’re unsure, put a question mark next to it or make it a different color on your digital calendar.
Just put it in a place so that it doesn’t have to be crammed in later.
Then for the other small things like candles and drinks and sweatshirts, simply be intentional.
Notice and enjoy.
Put on Nat King Cole.
Wear your cozy sweaters.
Light candles.
The small things have a lot of power, especially when bundled together, and it’s easy to forget that so here’s your reminder not to.
Don’t forget the power of small things.
When you get up in the morning, put on a great album, brew your coffee in your favorite mug with your pumpkin creamer, look out the window at the leaves, and just enjoy that moment of fall.
Let it turn you to gratitude.
Depending on your faith, even let it turn you to worship.
Let those small things mean something, not by forcing memories or magic but by simply letting them exist, make you smile, and make your day feel a little better.
It’s nice to be grateful for seasons that we love.
It’s good to be grateful for seasons we don’t love, but for fall, man is it fun to enjoy the simple things like soup and sweaters.
It’s not cliche even though it sounds like it.
You’re not basic or cliche.
You’re enjoying the little things in life that make you happy, and fall is full of them.
Enjoy it.
At first glance, this episode feels kind of basic and obvious.
Maybe it is.
But so often we’ll get midway through October and not have enjoyed any of our fall favorites with intention because we just didn’t take the time to think about them and schedule whatever we could.
It’s good work to do this.
It’s good work to notice your season, name what matters the most, put it in its place, and then enjoy it.
Plus it’s really fun.
Making your list will almost certainly be really fun.
So do that over the next day or two.
Make your fall favorites list.
Think about what you want to eat, drink, and cook.
Name your most essential fall activity and put it on the calendar.
Layer up those cozy aesthetics.
Think about books or movies or shows you want to rewatch or enjoy for the first time.
Let people into it.
Invite friends to come eat soup with you and watch When Harry Met Sally, and everyone wears their best fall sweater or brings their favorite cozy blanket.
Just do that, and that will make fall feel so special and something you likely look back on as a lovely memory.
Live in your season, and start small.
And that’s a fall bucket list but better.
After the break, we’ll have an Office Hours question about how to handle house rules when an older parent moves in and a great Lazy Genius of the Week with how to handle a random pocket of time.
We’ll be right back! *** AD BREAK *** This week’s Office Hours comes from Kelsey.
Kelsey asks: “My 80-year-old father has just moved in with my family (husband, 3 kids, and a dog), and I’m trying to navigate house rules with him.
He is an adult and really doesn’t have to listen to me the way my kids do, and it has caused some frustration for me (and only me), particularly in my kitchen.
The big one that is driving me particularly crazy is dishes sitting out to dry.
My husband and I recently made the agreement that we would wash and dry whatever dishes don’t fit in the dishwasher, rather than leaving them to dry, because it makes my life easier later.
But, naturally, my father just says, ‘let’s put a towel on the counter and let them dry, and we can put them away later/in the morning’ .
And then I walk into the kitchen in the morning to a counter FULL of dishes.
I couldn’t even reach the coffee pot this morning because of all the dishes.
So then I have to put dishes away before I even have my morning coffee (travesty).
I’m just wondering if you have any thoughts on how to get other adults on board for house rules. " That’s most definitely a challenge, Kelsey.
I don’t know how long your dad has been living with you, but it doesn’t sound like a long time.
Everyone’s lives are being upturned by this: yours, your family’s, your dad’s.
And clearly it’s top of mind because you said you couldn’t get to the coffee pot this morning.
You and your caffeine intake were impacted as early as today, at least the day you wrote this.
As I thought about how to answer your question, I put myself in your shoes because I would also prefer to have everyone who lives in one house to abide by the same House Rules, too.
It makes things easy for everyone.

But then I just kept imagining your dad and what a huge change it is to go from being an independent person who takes care of his family to needing to move in with you, his daughter, and live in a new place with new rhythms and his stuff in different places and figuring out how to make it his home, too.
That’s such an adjustment.
Chances are pretty good that the cycle of dishes doesn’t matter to him in the same way that they matter to you.
That’s a normal thing in homes where more than one person lives.
You’re going to have places where you disagree on what matters.
That’s really the foundation of it.
It’s not so much about adhering to House Rules.
It’s communicating what matters.
And that can be done in the moment.
In fact, when something matters more to you than it does to someone else, the onus of that choice is usually going to fall on your shoulders.
Not always but most of the time.
For example, my husband cares about laundry more than I do.
He fluffs pant legs midway through a drying cycle.
He cares about the temperature of the water.
Sometimes he’s come behind me while I’m putting in a load and starts to say specific things, and I’ll say, “Hey, you care more than I do, so why don’t you do it?” Not in a passive aggressive way.
In a legitimate problem-solving way.
Or flip it.
“I care more about this.

I’ll be happy to do it. ” I actually just read the book So You Married a Human by Jackie Kelley which is a marriage book with thirty rules for having an easier, more fun marriage, and one of her rules is similar: Do It Yourself.
Not in a sassy way.
It’s practical and kind.
If there is something we care about more than someone else we’re living with, chances are good we’ll do that thing more than they do.
So rather than trying to get your dad on board with drying dishes and putting them away, something he doesn’t care about so much, start by doing it yourself.
If your dad is washing the dishes and starts to leave them to dry on a towel, you can pop into the kitchen and start drying them and putting them away.
He might respond, “Oh honey, you don’t need to do that.
Just let them dry. ” And you can kindly say, “You know, it’s actually worth it to me to do it this way.
I love a clean counter in the morning. ” And just do it.

What often happens in situations like this is that whoever is washing the dishes and has watched you hand-dry and put them away over and over again starts to do it too because they are about you more than they care about the dishes.
They still don’t care about the clean counter as much, but they care about you and know you care about the counter.
I do that with Kaz and laundry now.
I ask him how he wants something washed if I’m doing a load he normally does.
Like our bath towels.
I know he washes them in a certain temperature, and I usually can’t remember what it is.

So if I’m taking that job for him because it’s been a busy week, I’ll say, “Remind me how you like to wash them” and then do it the way that matters to him because he matters to me more than the towels do.
This is not an automatic thing.
It’s not always immediate or becomes easy forever.
But this is the practice of being a person in a house with someone else.

You name what matters to you, and when that thing doesn’t matter as much to other people, you can communicate what matters as much as you can, but really you’ll probably need to do that thing awhile before your crew realizes how much it does actually matter.
Kaz wipes down the kitchen counters now because he knows how much it matters to me to come into the kitchen in the morning with a clean slate.
He didn’t used to do that.
The counters would be clear of stuff but not of dirt and stickiness.

So after weeks and months of me going back into the kitchen and cleaning the counters after he was done and us both communicating to each other that we weren’t mad, it just mattered a different amount, now he does it himself like 80% of the time because he knows it matters to me.
So kindly do it yourself while communicating why you’re doing it at all.
I think that eventually most people will come around and do what you need because they care about you, not the chore itself.
Hope that helps, Kelsey.
Alright, time for Lazy Genius of the Week!
This week we have Stephanie from New Rochelle, NY.
Stephanie writes: "I'm a freelancer and often purchase workshops, classes, etc. that I can never find time to watch!
I buy them because I know these classes have useful information but since I can't attend live, I figure I'll just watch the replay.
But I have a whole folder in my email of unwatched videos because in the grand scheme of my work day, other things are often more pressing and important than watching an hour-long workshop.

This fall my daughter will be taking two, 1 hour ballet classes a week and doing a 1 hour rehearsal of Nutcracker on the weekends, which is more than she's done in the past... which means I will have more time to kill!
It's too far to go back home so I'm deciding once.
These hours will be spent watching the workshops that have piled up!
It's easy to do right from my phone and I can bring earbuds and a small notebook with me.
If it's nice, I can sit outside the studio, and if not, there's a waiting area with plenty of seats.

I'm looking forward to not only watching the videos but also relieving myself of the decision fatigue of what to do each week during these 3+ hours!" I have an episode about this - Episode 322: What to Do with Random Pockets of Time because this is such a real challenge for so many people, and I love this solution for you, Stephanie.
You’re taking something that really can only exist in random pockets of time and putting it there in this new season with longer rehearsals.
Such a great idea, and I love how excited you are about it.
Thanks for sharing, and congratulations on being the Lazy Genius of the Week!
In the next podcast recap email, I’ll write out the golden milk process.
It is not hard, and like I said it’s deep in my Instagram feed, but I’ll pop what I normally do in there.
You can sign up for our recap email at thelazygeniuscollective.com/recap.
It goes out every other Thursday.
If this episode was helpful to you, share it with someone you know or leave a review on Apple Podcasts.
Both are small ways to support the show but hugely helpful to us, so thank you for your support.
This podcast is part of the Audacy family and the Office Ladies Network.
This episode is hosted by me, Kendra Adachi, produced by Leah Jarvis, and executive produced by Kendra Adachi, Jenna Fischer, and Angela Kinsey.
Thanks, y’all, for listening, and until next time, be a genius about the things that matter and lazy about the things that don’t.
I’m Kendra, and I’ll see you next week.

episodes.title: How to Fix Dinner When You’re Never Home (Rerun)

cues.text: #279 - How to Fix Dinner When You’re Never Home Hi there!
Welcome to the Lazy Genius Podcast!
I’m Kendra Adachi, and I’m here to help you be a genius about the things that matter and lazy about the things that don’t!
Today is episode 279 - how to fix dinner when you’re never home.
Welcome to fall, everyone!
The start of school, the rhythms and routines of a new season, the lowkey dread of the holidays that are far away but also not.
My Japanese father-in-law of all people said at dinner the other day that it’ll be Christmas before we know it.
He is not the demographic for that kind of sentiment, and yet he feels it too!
We are at the start of a lot, and it honestly already feels like the middle.
If you missed it, last week we talked about how to manage your time this fall.
That episode is an essential listen.
You don’t need to listen to it to make this one make sense or anything, but that episode is full of gold.
There are so many things that I loved creating, and the feedback I got last week confirmed it.
So if you didn’t listen to that episode, go back one and make sure you catch it.
The other thing I don’t want you to miss is The Holiday Docket which is the Lazy Genius GUide to Celebrating Well.
Basically if you want a path that helps you plan all of those holidays tasks and traditions and treasures, it is the resource for you.
We’ve had for three or four years now, and it is the top seller in our digital store for very good reason.
So check that out if you need holiday planning help.
But back to fall.
The point is that we have a lot of things we’re managing right now, and the one thing that never goes anywhere, no matter our season or stage of life, is food.
We have to eat, you guys.
I love to eat so much, so it’s not exactly true for me to say that it’d be great if we didn’t have to worry about it.
But I also get why it would be easier not to worry about it.
If someone could just serve me food everyday, that would be ideal.
But since that is not the ideal for the majority of people, we have to figure it out.
And this time of the year is possibly the hardest to figure out.
We go from summer where food rules are looser.
We’re grilling or eating at the pool or trying to figure out how to not turn on the oven.
Kids are home, snacking is prevalent, it’s all just easier.
It has its own set of challenges, but part of the vibe of summer food is ease.
No stress, baby.
But also most of us prefer cooking in the fall and winter, in cooler weather, because we can make recipes and meals that we’re generally more comfortable with, like soup and stuff.
In fact, the challenge in feeding yourself and your people in the fall isn’t a lack of recipes.
It very much isn’t.
The challenge for many of you is that we’re never home.
This episode is likely geared mostly toward families with kids simply because that’s where most of the activity comes from.
But I have a friend who is single and has no kids and spends three or four nights a week doing extracurricular stuff with friends.

She works late one or two nights, and then one night she’s in an adult kickball league, another she plays volleyball I think… the point is that you don’t have to have kids to feel like you’re never home.
If you do have kids, especially ones that are older but cannot drive themselves around yet, it is a cluster.
Our weeks right now include two working parents with jobs, piano lessons, youth group, math tutoring, and dance class.
In the next month, we will also likely be adding saxophone lessons, after school art classes four days a week, LEGO club, and a night class I’m taking.
You guys.
What is happening.
I’ve had this conversation with several friends recently, especially parents with more than one kid.
Even if every kid has just one thing they do, it’s still a ton of things to manage every week.
And so many kids play a sport and an instrument or are in a club and taking tutoring or whatever.
Most kids aren’t even doing just the one thing.

Obviously, you can set limits in your own family based on what matters to you, but a friend of mine who like me loves being at home with her family, who seeks to have pretty peaceful home life with not a lot of extra still finds it to be almost too much.
And we’re doing almost a bare minimum by many standards.
So first, you’re doing great.
This season feels like a cluster because you have a lot of stuff on the calendar, most of which is crammed between 4 and 8pm.
It’s unfair.
But it’s also the reality.
So today we start with kindness towards ourselves and our people, keeping resentment at bay for quote being in this mess.
It’s likely no one’s fault.
Everyone is just trying to feel like themselves, and the more people in your house, the more activities are needed to meet everyone’s needs.
It’s normal and hard and normal.
So in light of all of that, how do we cook dinner?
How do we make sure everybody eats when we never seem to be home at actual dinner time or even at the same time?
Again, a cluster.
Here’s what we normally do.
We start with the recipe, with the what.
What are we going to have for dinner?
We Google “dinners to take to the ball field” or “dinner made the night before” or whatever, knowing that we barely have energy to wash our face the night before, let alone make an entire meal.
Or we start with the how, with the hacks and the special coolers and the meal plans specifically made for the busiest people!
And sometimes those things work.
For sure.
But we start with what and how, and I think that’s starting in the wrong place.
For once, I’m not going to tell you to start with what matters.
Shocker, I know.
Were you expecting a juke where I’m like that’s where you start, guys.
Nope, not this time.
I mean, yeah, it’s great to know what matters, but my guess is it’s some version of I just need everybody to eat, fast food is acceptable, but not every night.
Does that sound about right?
We want ease, we want automation, we want flavor and enjoyment, and we want togetherness.
But we’re also realistic grownups who know that we likely cannot have all of those things every single night, especially during soccer season or whatever.
So here’s where I want you to start when you’re trying to fix dinner but you’re never home.
I want you to start with when, where, and who.
All at once because it’s probably easier that way since they all impact the other.
But first start with when, where, and who.
When will you eat?
Where will you eat?
Who is going to eat together at that time?
We’ll be right back…
All of these make sense - the when, where, and who, but let’s break them down just a touch.
When will you eat dinner?
I think this is more flexible than you think.
My suggestion is for you to set the time frame, but it’s likely that any time between school letting out and your absolute latest dinner time is open for business.
You don’t have to eat dinner at 6pm every single night is what I’m saying.
You don’t even have to eat what you consider dinner foods as dinner every single night.
I think that’s actually the problem: you think you should fit a crazy season of life into a different season, more predictable season of life.
Dinner should be this kind of meal at this time of day, and if things are off of that ideal, you’re doing it wrong.
This is just not true.
If you are a sports mom, if you are Erin H.
Moon, expecting a standard dinner to happen at 6pm every night with the entire family is unreasonable and crazy-making.
If you are in a sports mom season or whatever your season is, you need to live in it.
And part of that is widening the field of when dinner happens.
The other thing is the where.

You can eat at home, in the car when it’s moving, in the car when it’s stopped, on public transportation if that’s how you get around, at the field or studio or classroom, at a restaurant, or at somebody else’s home.
The combination of the where and the when is essential.
We will eat at 4pm at home before everybody takes off for their things.
We will eat at 7pm in the car on the way home from everybody’s things.
We will eat in the parking lot of a restaurant in between everybody’s things.
Where and when.
Look at the day and decide where and when dinner is best.
So if we want to systemize this, I’d like you to look at your life maybe one week at a time.
During a season when you feel like you’re never home and life is unpredictable, start small with one week at a time.
Don’t build the whole system based on your first week.
Start small.
Try it for a week and see what happens.
You are also more likely to continue this system of one week at a time by deciding once when you’re going to do it.
I believe that having a consistent day or time to look at this will really help you.
Put it in a routine or on your calendar.
So when it’s time to look at the week and make a plan for dinner, go day by day.
When and where?
Based on the practices and games and club meetings and lessons and whatever else is happening, when and where does dinner make the most sense?
And obviously the ideal who is everybody.

Everybody eats dinner together, but that’s not going to always happen, so you can also consider the who in this process and either adjust dinnertime to fit everyone or make a plan for the person won’t be there or if they’re old enough tell them to make the plan.
“You’re on your own for dinner on Thursday, Charlie.
You need anything?” or whatever.
One more note about choosing when and where.
The when can be a specific time, a range, or a time related to another activity.

For example, if you say that on Wednesday you’re going to eat at 7pm because soccer practice ends at 6:30pm and yes that’s later than you’d like but it’s the season we’re in, but then your daughter is hanging out with a teammate or two after practice and you’re like girl come on we need to get home for dinner we need to eat at 7pm!
You’re paying attention to the clock.

But what if instead on that particular day, you didn’t say 7pm but you said “after soccer practice. ” And maybe your daughter has had a hard time making friends on this team so her hanging out with a couple of teammates is actually really great and worth waiting for and you don’t want to rush it.
And you don’t have to because you’ve already decided you’re having dinner after practice, not at 7.
So for each day, ask yourself, when and where will we eat?
And will everybody be there?
Once that is decided, now you can figure out the what and the how.

If you start with what, you’re trying to figure out how to take chili - usually a very easy meal to make at home - to softball practice and dripping it down your sweater because you’re dragging a crockpot out of the trunk of the car.
I’m not making this up.
I have seen parents with crockpots in the trunks of cars.
There is nothing wrong with that choice.
But so often when we start with the meal, with the recipe, with the what, we go in the wrong order.
So we’ve started with where, when, and who.
That will inform your what and your how.
You don’t have to take chili in a crockpot in the trunk of the car.
Unless you just really want to, then go for it.
So again, we’re starting with one week at a time.
Do not build this big.
Start with this week that’s in front of you.
You have written down where and when you’ll eat.
Now let’s figure out what.
I want you to avoid searching through the treasure trove of all the recipes you’ve ever made and forcing them into this season.
Instead, guess what you need?
A dinner queue.
You need I’m Never Home Dinner Queue or a Sports Season Dinner Queue or something.
What are meal ideas that fit in the when and where you’re already thinking about?
Look at the meals you already made, that everyone already likes, that are your Brainless Crowdpleasers.
Which ones would work in this season, at least or certain when/where combinations?
Maybe chili is still a great option because you can make it in the crockpot or whatever and have it ready, but maybe you don’t bring it in a crockpot.
Maybe you have thermoses that you fill with chili in the 15 minutes you’re home between school and practice.
Take them with you.
They’re ready for whoever needs them.
Maybe you can do Snack Platters or pack picnic things that can be eaten without silverware.
Maybe you cook the Sloppy Joe stuff in the morning or the night before when you’re already in the kitchen for yesterday’s dinner and just heat it up in a skillet or the microwave when you get home.
In fact, the whats might not be change that much.
It’s really the how.
How are you going to make this food or gather this food or pack this food to match the when and the where?
So much of this is my favorite thing ever which is reverse engineering.
Start at the end.
Which we already did.
Start with the when and the where.
Now move backwards.
When will you grab the food in order to eat it at that time and in that place?
Will you cook it then?
Will you cook it earlier?
Can cooking that meal coincide with cooking the one from the night before?
Can you get into a rhythm during this season of prepping some of tomorrow’s meal during today’s?
Do you see how starting with the when and the where really turbocharges everything else?

It helps you name what you need, what you don’t, what you have time for, how often you need to shop, how important it is to eat a homemade dinner at home on Saturday nights or have Sunday breakfast or some fixed point for your entire family because the rest of the week is crazy?
But having that fixed point lessens the guilt of relying on convenience and takeout more often?
You can’t cram a different season into “sports” season.
You can’t do it.
You’ll drive yourself crazy.
You’ll feel bad about the whole thing.
You’ll be frustrated at your people for being involved in too many things.
You’ll be desperate for the season to be over, or you’ll deal with it by making choices that don’t align with what matters to you.
So instead name what matters, and go in the right order.
Start with the when and the where.
Decide once when you make a plan.
Create a busy season dinner queue.
Pull from that.
Be creative.
Don’t think it’s weird if you’re eating a full meal at 3:30pm after school and snacking later.
That’s not weird that’s being an excellent problem solver.
And then reverse engineer how you can make that meal happen in a way where your - listen up - where your expectations match the energy you’re willing to give.
I said that in the episode a few weeks ago about making work lunches, and the same is very true.
Match your expectations with the energy you’re willing to give them.
But the little sparkly key here?
Start with when and where.
And that’s how to fix dinner when you’re never home.
Before we go, let’s celebrate the Lazy Genius of the Week!
This week it’s my buddy Anna Sale.
Anna Sale is the author of Let’s Talk About Hard Things and host of the podcast Death, Sex, and Money.
She is a delightful human who I have loved getting to know, and she sent me this text last week.
“I need you to know, I asked my children to put on their shoes BEFORE breakfast instead of right after when it’s time to leave for school and we were five minutes earlier in leaving.
A LAZY GENIUS HACK FOR THE WIN. ” I share this for two reasons.
One, it’s a great idea.
Shoes are a whole thing.
I mean, I have an entire episode on shoes, most of which is how to get our kids to put them on and lose them less often.
So putting shoes on before breakfast when things aren’t harried is going in the right order.
Such a great idea and likely one that a lot of you might be excited to try.
And the second reason I share it is because of how fun it is to discover something that seems so small but is so life-changing and then share it with someone else.
Anna was excited about this new shoe discovery and texted me her excitement, and I got to be excited right alongside her.
Sharing your tiny wins along with your frustrations and the mundane is what makes relationships go.
So pick a pal and text them your little win.
It’s good for everybody when you do.
So congratulations, Anna Sale, on being our Lazy Genius of the week.
Okay, y’all, that’s it for today!
Thanks so much for listening, and I hope you’re walking away with a tool or two to help you fix dinner even though you’re never home.
And if you enjoyed this episode, it would be amazing if you would share it with someone you think would like it.
This podcast has always been an organic grower, and that’s because of shares like yours.
So thanks for passing it along to someone you think would be into it.
Alright, y’all, thanks for listening, and until next time, be a genius about the things that matter and lazy about the things that don’t.
I’m Kendra, and I’ll see you next week!

For more information, visit teacherluke.co.uk Hello listeners, welcome back to Luke's English Podcast.
How are you doing today?
I hope you're doing fine.
Welcome to this brand new episode.
And today on the podcast, I would like to celebrate the life of a living legend, and that is Sir David Attenborough.
Have you ever heard of David Attenborough?
Do you know who he is?
If you look at the PDF for this, I've added a photograph at the top, and you'll see David sitting in a chair.
And then another picture behind him, which is him in 1979, lying down on some grass in the jungle with a gorilla sitting on top of him, a young gorilla.
And this is a picture from one of the most amazing moments in television that I remember seeing on TV a few times.
And it was just an absolutely incredible moment when David and a BBC camera crew went to Rwanda, went to the jungle in Rwanda and filmed very closely a family of gorillas.
And it was an incredible moment because obviously you think these creatures might be dangerous and also quite shy.
And yet David and his crew managed to get really close to them and film them.
And not only that, they ended up interacting with him.
One of the young ones decided to climb all over him and play with him.
And the mother gorilla who was sitting just next to them at one point grabbed David's head and turned his head with her big hand and stared right into his eyes.
And that was just one of the most brilliant moments of television that David was involved in or has been involved in in his life.
And I'll talk more about that gorilla encounter in this episode, as well as lots of other incredible moments with animals that I saw and so many people have seen in his documentaries over the years.
So Sir David Attenborough is the name of the episode and also the subject of this episode.

So this will be a rambling tribute to this British gentleman who so many of us know and love, or most of us don't know him personally, of course, but we kind of feel like we do because we listen to him as children when he spoke to us every week in our living rooms on television.

Luke’s English Podcast - teacherluke.co.uk Sir David Attenborough 🌍 Britain's #1 National Treasure [1005] Episode Transcript 2 In terms of language learning opportunities with this episode, because this is a podcast for learners of English, of course, look out for English for describing someone's character, achievements and career, descriptions of animals, including their behaviour and habitat, the language of conservationism, environmental awareness and various personal reflections and anecdotes and rambling memories from me, which I will attempt to put clearly into words and sentences in English, of course.
I'm sure the episode will be rich with vocabulary and perhaps some complex grammar here and there as I attempt to do justice to this man through my words.
So, plenty for you to feed on in terms of nutrient-rich language input for the development of your English.
Sir David Attenborough, yes.
And now perhaps I should mention my ex-girlfriend at the start of this episode, just to get your attention.
Shall I talk about my ex-girlfriend just to get your attention?
It seemed to work with last week's episode.
Actually, there is a connection with last week's episode of this podcast which I retold the story of Jurassic Park from the point of view of one of the characters.
